# Welcome {-}

How many patients would you need to compare a new pain treatment with standard treatment? This tutorial helps you justify a sample size that can answer your research question, using clinical examples, calculations and simulation.

Although the examples are clinical, the principles of justifying assumptions, choosing a target difference, and examining power and precision also apply in psychology, education, and other quantitative disciplines [@lakens2022]. The tutorial is a suitable starting point for learning these principles and planning comparisons of two independent groups with a continuous or binary outcome, provided the calculation’s assumptions match your study. Later chapters introduce other planning goals and help you recognize when a different method is needed. For factorial experiments and repeated-measures ANOVA, including designs common in psychology, *[Power Analysis with Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/)* provides more directly applicable examples and simulations [@superpowerbook2022]. Studies involving multilevel models, prediction, or time-to-event outcomes need guidance matched to those analyses; the chapter [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) points you toward relevant resources. What counts as a worthwhile difference should also reflect your field and research question.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

This tutorial is for students and researchers. Chapters 1–3 form the Core route for basic two-arm trial planning. Chapters 4–8 offer Advanced topics that you can consult according to your study question. The glossary and common questions are reference pages for either route.

Activities are learning exercises; apps are the software used to carry them out. The roadmap links the reading, activities and apps. Expandable misconception boxes explain common difficulties as they arise.

```{r tutorial-roadmap, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
roadmap <- paste(readLines("../figures/tutorial-roadmap.svg",
  encoding="UTF-8", warn=FALSE), collapse="\n")
# Numeric entities keep SVG text intact when R uses a non-UTF-8 locale.
roadmap <- paste(vapply(utf8ToInt(enc2utf8(roadmap)), function(cp) {
  if (cp > 127L) sprintf("&#%d;", cp) else intToUtf8(cp)
}, character(1)), collapse="")
cat('<figure class="tutorial-roadmap">',
    roadmap, '</figure>')
```

Chapter quizzes and the [cumulative quiz](#cumulative-quiz) help you check your understanding. The [activity walkthroughs](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/activity-walkthroughs.html) provide additional guidance when needed.

The three core chapters develop one [sample size calculation report](#reporting), with a supporting study plan. Advanced chapters extend the calculations to estimation, uncertain assumptions, simulation and other study designs.

[Flashcards](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/index.html) are available for Core and Core + Advanced, with a [question-and-answer preview](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/cards.html) and Anki/Quizlet downloads. Questions and suggestions are welcome through [Feedback](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/j00AMibqi5).

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
## Core learning outcomes {#core-route .unnumbered .core-heading}

The linked sections should help you develop a sample size justification for a basic two-arm trial. By the end, you should be able to:

- [Define a clinical question and justify assumptions](#clinical-question), distinguishing the [difference observed in previous data](#expected-difference), [target difference](#target-difference) and [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold).
- [Explain Type I error probability, Type II error probability and power](#power).
- Use [one simulated study and many studies](#activity-1-one-study-then-many) to distinguish [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) from [population parameters](#population-parameter) and see how results vary.
- [Calculate sample size for two proportions or two means](#calculations) and [adjust recruitment for expected losses](#account-for-expected-losses), distinguishing analyzable counts from recruitment counts.
- Explain why a sample size requirement depends on its [specified assumptions](#calculations).
- [Write a short sample size justification](#write-a-sample-size-justification) recording assumptions, calculation and recruitment, using [your continuing report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question).

:::

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
## Advanced learning outcomes {#advanced-route .unnumbered .advanced-heading}

The extensions below may be relevant to your study question. They should help you:

- Plan a [prevalence estimate](#prevalence) or [population mean estimate](#plan-for-precision) for a useful confidence interval width, and [interpret intervals clinically](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically).
- Distinguish [an observed significance boundary from planned power](#critical-observed-difference) and explore [sampling distributions and error regions](#alpha-beta).
- [Read power curves](#curves), assess [plausible alternative assumptions](#stress-test-the-study-plan), and explain the consequences of [low power](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose).
- [Build a simulated clinical trial](#simulation) to examine power, coverage and precision, accounting for [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error).
- Assess [existing-data reuse](#dataset-reuse), [rare-disease constraints](#rare-diseases), and the information needed for decisions in a [pilot or feasibility study](#pilot-feasibility).
- Recognize [study designs that need another method](#study-designs), including paired measurements and prediction models.
- Explain how [multiple comparisons](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), [interim analyses](#interim-analyses-stopping) and [sample-size re-estimation](#sample-size-re-estimation) affect planning and reporting.
- [Reproduce calculations and simulations](#appendix) with their assumptions and methods documented.

:::


# Research question and power {#clinical-question .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Specify a clinical question, outcome, design and planned comparison.
- Distinguish a difference observed in earlier data, a calculation target and a clinical threshold.
- Explain Type I and Type II error probabilities and power under specified assumptions.
- Use one study and repeated studies to explain sampling variability and the effect of sample size.
:::

## The chronic pain trial: how many patients do you need? {#the-chronic-pain-study-how-many-patients-do-we-need .core-heading}

Suppose you are a clinician caring for people with chronic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. You identify a promising drug candidate, Neravixa—a fictional medicine for this example—and want to investigate whether it helps more patients achieve pain relief than duloxetine, an established treatment [@emaduloxetine].

A small [pilot study](#pilot-study) found that 7 of 10 patients receiving Neravixa achieved pain relief, compared with 3 of 10 receiving duloxetine: 70% versus 30%, an observed difference of 40 [percentage points](#percentage-points). This is a promising result, but the difference is uncertain because so few patients were studied.

You plan a larger trial in which eligible patients will be randomly assigned in equal numbers to Neravixa or duloxetine. The [primary outcome](#primary-outcome) at four weeks is [binary](#binary-outcome): each patient either achieved measurable pain relief or did not, using the same assessment in both groups. Subsequent examples use the shorter labels “achieved pain relief” and “did not achieve pain relief.” Neravixa is the novel treatment and duloxetine the standard treatment throughout this case.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-pilot-patients) illustrates these pilot results.

```{r pain-pilot-patients, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.7, fig.cap="Illustration of the hypothetical pilot: ten patients per treatment group start with pain. Downward arrows lead to their outcomes at four weeks. Green figures with raised arms indicate reported pain relief; red figures indicate no reported relief at follow-up. The counts describe this small pilot sample.", fig.alt="Two treatment groups: standard treatment on the left and novel treatment on the right. Each is shown before treatment and after a downward arrow marking four weeks. All ten patients in each group start red, indicating pain. In the standard-treatment group, three of ten become green with raised arms, indicating reported pain relief, and seven remain red. In the novel-treatment group, seven of ten become green and three remain red. Pain relief is reported by 30% with standard treatment and 70% with novel treatment."}
draw_pain_pilot_patients()
```

How many patients would this trial need to have a high probability of detecting a clinically worthwhile difference? In this tutorial, you will work through the decisions behind that calculation and explore the results that different repetitions of the trial could produce.

This first section focuses on two-arm randomized superiority trials: patients are assigned by chance to one of two treatment groups, and the aim is to investigate whether one treatment performs better than the other. The core calculations cover binary and continuous outcomes. The separate [estimation chapter](#estimation-planning) uses a precision target; later chapters address other designs.

The following sections develop the question and assumptions that determine the calculation in Chapter 2.

## Why does sample size matter? {#what-should-this-study-establish .core-heading}

A sample size calculation helps assess what the planned study could establish under its assumptions. Too few patients may leave a clinically worthwhile difference undetected; unnecessary recruitment adds participant burden and time. The proposed trial needs a meaningful question, sufficient power for its intended comparison, and a feasible recruitment plan.

### Ethical review and the study protocol {.core-heading}

A scientifically sound study is an ethical requirement. The Declaration of Helsinki sets out international ethical principles, including scientific validity, a justified [study protocol](#study-protocol), and prior [research ethics committee](#research-ethics-committee) review [@wmahelsinki2024]. Your protocol should explain the proposed sample size, the evidence behind its assumptions, and the information expected in relation to participants' burden and risk.

For clinical trials of medicines, the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) provides a shared statistical framework used worldwide in its [E9 guideline](#ich-e9). Its sample-size guidance calls for an explicit outcome, target difference, analysis, error probabilities and assumptions, with sensitivity to uncertainty considered [@iche91998].

Review procedures depend on the country and study type. Your institution's research office or ethics committee should help identify the applicable requirements. The following are regional and national examples:

- European Union: clinical trials of medicines within the scope of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 require scientific and ethical review; ethics committees operate under the law of the relevant member state [@ecethicsreview]. Other study types follow their applicable frameworks.
- Netherlands: research within the [Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO)](#wmo) framework is reviewed by an accredited [medical research ethics committee (METC)](#metc) or the [Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects (CCMO)](#ccmo), as applicable [@ccmowmo].
- United States: an [institutional review board (IRB)](#institutional-review-board) reviews studies subject to the relevant human-participant protections. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements apply to covered clinical investigations; Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) regulations apply to covered research conducted or supported by HHS [@fdairb2025; @hhsresearchreview].

<span id="ethics-sample-size"></span>

## Defining the research question and study design {#how-do-you-determine-the-minimum-required-sample-size .core-heading}

A sample size calculation supports these scientific and ethical judgments when it addresses a clearly defined research question. PICO identifies the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome, including the assessment time [@richardson1995]. For the chronic pain trial:

| PICO element | Specification |
|:--|:--|
| Population | Adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus, bilateral lower-extremity pain attributable to diabetic peripheral neuropathy for at least one year, and body mass index (BMI) ≥18 and <40 kg/m². |
| Intervention | Neravixa, the novel treatment. |
| Comparator | Duloxetine, the standard treatment. |
| Outcome | Achieved pain relief at four weeks: yes or no, assessed in the same way in both groups. |

Table: (\#tab:pain-pico) The clinical question for the chronic pain trial, specified using PICO.

Participants will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to two [independent groups](#independent-groups). Each person contributes one outcome; bilateral pain does not create two independent participants. The comparison concerns the absolute difference between the groups' pain-relief percentages. The planned analysis compares two independent proportions using a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test).

Guidance for the study design helps identify decisions to document before choosing calculation inputs [@fong2026; @wang2020]. For randomized trials, [SPIRIT](#spirit) 2025 covers protocols and [CONSORT](#consort) 2025 covers reporting results [@spiritconsort2025]. The chapter [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) links to guidance for other designs, including [STROBE](#strobe) for observational studies and [STARD](#stard) for diagnostic accuracy.

The map provides an overview of the remaining planning decisions. Its short explanations link to the sections where each decision is developed.

```{r study-questions-map, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::asis_output(render_question_map())
```

## Pilot findings, target difference, and clinical importance {#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically .core-heading}

The pilot findings provide a starting point for planning the larger trial. Three quantities help organize the reasoning: the difference observed in the pilot, the target difference used in the calculation, and the clinical threshold. All three concern differences between groups.

The [difference observed in the pilot](#expected-difference) is 40 percentage points: 70% achieved pain relief with Neravixa, compared with 30% with duloxetine. This describes the patients in that small study. Another pilot could produce a different result. These findings should therefore be considered alongside other relevant evidence, including differences in pain severity, background treatment and assessment time.

The [target difference](#target-difference) is the population difference at which the sample size calculation evaluates [power](#statistical-power). The trial is planned for a target difference of 30 percentage points: 60% pain relief with Neravixa versus 30% with duloxetine. The sample size will be chosen to give 90% power under these assumptions. Choosing the target requires a judgment about what difference is plausible and important to detect; the uncertain pilot estimate is one source of evidence [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2].

The [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) is the smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile. For this teaching case, suppose Neravixa requires four additional safety-monitoring visits and carries a risk of short-lived dizziness. Patient and clinical advisers judge that at least 20 additional patients achieving pain relief per 100 treated would justify this additional burden and potential harm compared with duloxetine. This gives a clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The judgment needs to reflect the particular treatments and patients [@cook2018delta2].

These values serve different purposes and may coincide or follow a different numerical order in another study. They describe comparisons between groups. The section [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) explains why they cannot describe the benefit for each individual patient.

| Quantity | Value | Role in this study |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Difference observed in the pilot | 40 percentage points: 70% versus 30% | Sample result that informs planning, with uncertainty |
| Target between-group difference | 30 percentage points: 60% versus 30% | Population difference at which the calculation evaluates power |
| Clinically worthwhile between-group difference (clinical threshold) | 20 percentage points | Smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile, considering burdens, risks, and alternatives |

Table: (\#tab:pain-planning-values) Earlier observations and two planning decisions for the chronic pain trial; their numerical values can coincide.

Figure \@ref(fig:planning-differences) places these values on the same scale. All are absolute differences in percentage points. Labels such as small, medium or large leave the clinical meaning unspecified [@caldwell2020].

The advanced section [Choosing plausible assumptions](#st01-expectations) discusses how previous findings, target differences, and clinical judgments inform a study plan.

```{r planning-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Difference observed in the pilot, target difference and clinical threshold for the chronic pain trial. The pilot value is a sample result; the target and threshold concern population differences. All are expressed in percentage points. Their values may coincide or follow a different order in other studies.", fig.alt="Three compact horizontal rows share an axis for novel minus standard treatment. Each line starts at zero and ends at its labeled value: difference observed in the pilot, 40 percentage points, calculated from the pilot patients; target difference, 30 points, used to evaluate power; clinical threshold, 20 points, the smallest benefit judged worthwhile."}
draw_planning_differences()
```

The sample size is chosen to give 90% power at the 30-point target difference. With the same sample size, standard-treatment response percentage and test, power is lower at a true 20-point difference, even though that benefit would still matter clinically. A larger sample is needed to achieve 90% power for that smaller difference. The next section explains power and the two error probabilities.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-effect">
<summary>Common misconception: the pilot reveals the true treatment effect</summary>

If another pilot found relief in 8 of 10 patients receiving Neravixa and 3 of 10 receiving duloxetine, its observed difference would be 50 percentage points. That new sample result would add evidence to the planning decision. The target difference would still need justification using all relevant findings and clinical importance [@albers2018].

</details>


<details class="misconception" id="model-answer-pilot-threshold">
<summary>Common misconception: the clinical threshold should follow the pilot result</summary>

If the pilot had shown relief in 6 rather than 7 treated patients, should the clinical threshold change?

The observed difference would fall from 40 to 30 percentage points, with standard-treatment relief still at 30%. That changes the evidence about the likely benefit. The clinical threshold remains 20 points because the judgment about worthwhile relief, harms and burden has not changed.

</details>

## Hypotheses, error probabilities, and power {#power .core-heading}

<span id="hypotheses-and-error-probabilities"></span>

The [null hypothesis](#null-hypothesis) says that the population pain-relief percentages are equal. The [alternative hypothesis](#alternative-hypothesis) allows a difference in either direction. A statistically significant result provides evidence against the null hypothesis under the test's assumptions.

Let $\delta$ denote the population difference: Neravixa minus duloxetine. Positive values favor Neravixa and negative values favor duloxetine. The two-sided test compares:

\begin{equation}
H_0: \delta=0, \qquad H_1: \delta\ne0.
(\#eq:hypotheses)
\end{equation}

A test's decision can agree or disagree with the population truth. The table shows the four possibilities.

```{r error-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Decision = c("Statistically significant difference (reject the null)", "No statistically significant difference (do not reject the null)"),
  `No population difference` = c("False positive (Type I error)", "True negative"),
  `Specified population difference exists` = c("True positive", "False negative (Type II error)"),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Testing decisions across repeated studies.")
```

[Type I error probability](#alpha) is the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis: a [false positive](#false-positive). Here, it means finding a statistically significant difference when the population pain-relief probabilities are equal. A 5% Type I error probability corresponds to about 5 false positives per 100 repetitions when the null hypothesis is true, under the test's assumptions.

[Type II error probability](#beta) is the probability of failing to reject the null hypothesis at a specified true difference: a [false negative](#false-negative). Power is the probability of detecting that difference, equal to 1 minus the Type II error probability. If the population relief percentages are 60% and 30%, a study with 90% power would detect a difference in about 90 of 100 repetitions and miss it in about 10. Calculations or simulations estimate this probability; the trial itself is conducted once.

The sample size calculation evaluates power at the specified 30-point difference. The test evaluates the evidence against a population difference of zero.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means a 90% probability that the treatment works</summary>

Power assumes a particular true difference and describes the planned test's performance across repeated studies. A study with 90% power can still miss that difference.

</details>

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-Type I error probability-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: Type I error probability of 5% means a significant result has a 5% probability of being a false positive</summary>

The 5% probability applies to studies in which the null hypothesis is true. The percentage of significant findings that are false positives also depends on how often real differences exist and on the studies' power.

</details>

A false positive could contribute to adopting a treatment that adds burden without improving pain relief. A false negative could delay recognition of a worthwhile benefit. These consequences, alongside methodological and regulatory guidance, inform the chosen error probabilities. The chronic pain plan uses a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and 90% power.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

What would change if the trial needed 90% power when the true treatment difference was 20 percentage points?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-target-choice">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A trial sized for 90% power at a 30-point difference has lower power at a true 20-point difference. Planning for 90% power at 20 points requires a larger sample and reduces the probability of failing to detect that smaller, worthwhile benefit.

The choice depends on which difference the trial needs a high probability of detecting. The clinical threshold stays at 20 points in either plan. [Chapter 2](#two-proportions) shows the numerical consequences.

</details>
:::

## One study and many studies {#activity-1-one-study-then-many .core-heading}

The pilot observed 70% versus 30% relief. The simulation explores the planning assumption of population probabilities of 60% with Neravixa and 30% with duloxetine. This makes the population difference known, so the results of individual trials can be compared with it.

### Three trials under the same assumptions {#a-couple-of-individual-trials .core-heading}

Three simulated trials each include 20 patients per group and follow the same study design. Each trial generates a different set of patient outcomes. Consequently, the numbers achieving pain relief—and the observed difference between treatments—can vary. Figure \@ref(fig:three-pain-trials) follows each trial from its patient outcomes to its estimated treatment difference.

```{r pain-sample-estimates}
# <- saves a result under a name. lapply() repeats the same steps for each trial.
# The population probabilities stay fixed; each run generates new patients.
example_trials <- lapply(20260941:20260943, function(trial_seed) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 20,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    seed = trial_seed)
  simulate_one_study(scenario)
})
# Combine one row per trial into a table. [[i]] selects trial i from the list.
trial_examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(example_trials), function(i) {
  trial <- example_trials[[i]]
  # For 0/1 outcomes, the mean within each group is its observed relief fraction.
  rates <- tapply(trial$data$outcome, trial$data$group, mean)
  data.frame(Trial = i, `Duloxetine: achieved pain relief` = percent(rates["Control"]),
    `Neravixa: achieved pain relief` = percent(rates["Treatment"]),
    `Observed difference` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$estimate), " percentage points"),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
# kable() formats the results as a readable table.
knitr::kable(trial_examples, caption = "Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group, all sampled under the same 30% and 60% population event probabilities.")
```

```{r three-pain-trials, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap="Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group. All use the same population pain-relief probabilities: 30% with duloxetine and 60% with Neravixa. Filled circles show achieved pain relief; open circles show no pain relief. Arrows connect each pair of groups to its observed difference. The dashed line marks the population difference of 30 percentage points.", fig.alt="Three rows show individual patient outcomes in the duloxetine and Neravixa groups, their relief counts and percentages, and the resulting treatment differences on a shared scale. The patient outcomes and estimates vary while the population difference stays at 30 percentage points."}
draw_three_pain_trials(example_trials)
```

These trials share population probabilities, group sizes, allocation and testing procedure. Their patient outcomes, observed percentages, differences and decisions vary. The simulation makes the distinction between population and sample visible because its population parameters are known.

### Many trials and a larger sample {.core-heading}

Repeating the trial 5,000 times shows a range of possible sample differences. As a rule, larger samples produce less variable estimates. Across repeated trials, their estimates are more tightly clustered around the population difference.

```{r three-samples}
# c() collects the three patient counts to compare.
sample_sizes <- c(20, 50, 80)
# Repeat 5,000 trials at each count; n is patients per group, B is trials.
batches <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = n,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    width_target = .20, B = 5000, seed = 20260921 + n)
  simulate_trials(scenario)
})
# Extract and combine each batch's percentage of significant results.
power_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, power_row))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Statistically significant results` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Percentage of 5,000 simulated trials detecting the assumed 30-percentage-point population difference at each sample size.")
```

```{r sample-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Observed treatment differences across 5,000 simulated trials at each sample size. The dashed line marks the specified population difference of 30 percentage points. As a rule, larger samples produce less variable estimates.", fig.alt="Three histograms of observed relief differences with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, showing progressively narrower distributions around the same population difference of 30 percentage points."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  for (batch in batches) {
    hist(100 * batch$results$estimate, breaks = seq(-100, 100, 5),
      xlim = c(-40, 90), col = "#b9d4f3", border = "white",
      main = paste(batch$spec$n, "patients per group"),
      xlab = "Observed difference in relief (percentage points)", ylab = "Number of trials")
    abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#69509a")
  }
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:sample-differences) shows [sampling variability](#sampling-variability); the table shows how often the planned test detects the specified population difference. The assumed true difference here equals the 30-point [target difference](#target-difference) used to evaluate power. The simulation uses the specified population probabilities of 30% and 60%.

<span id="model-answer-sample-versus-population"></span>

Increasing the sample size changes the information in each trial. Increasing simulation repetitions makes the estimated percentage of significant results more stable; each trial retains the same sample size and power.

The app below generates further trials from these same 30% and 60% populations. It starts with 20 patients per group, matching the first illustrated trials. It also displays the calculated requirement of 56 per group for 90% power, explained in [Two proportions](#two-proportions); that count can be used directly in the simulation. Comparing the resulting dots and repeated-study graph shows what the extra patients change.

```{r pain-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_one_many", "Simulate further trials and compare different sample sizes.",
  image = "../figures/pain-trials-preview.png")
```

This repeated-study approach follows the introductory teaching idea in @superpowerbook2022 and the use of simulation in health-sciences education [@thiesmeier2024; @rudolph2021]. The [advanced simulation explanation](#precision-of-a-simulation) examines how precisely a simulation estimates study performance.

The advanced chapter on [power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) explains the sampling-distribution diagrams and the pilot's significance boundary. The simple simulation here provides the background needed for the basic calculations.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- A sample size calculation starts with the research question and planned analysis.
- A pilot result describes its sample; relevant evidence and uncertainty inform the main study assumptions.
- Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference.
- More patients change a study's power; more simulation repetitions make its estimated performance more stable.
- The target difference and clinical threshold have distinct roles and may have the same value.

</div>

# Calculating sample size and recruitment {#calculations .core-heading}


::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain how the [target difference](#target-difference), [event probabilities](#event-probability) or [standard deviation](#standard-deviation), [Type I error probability](#alpha), and target [power](#statistical-power) affect sample size.
- Calculate the [analyzable sample size](#analyzable-sample-size) for two independent proportions or means.
- Interpret per-group and total counts, including upward rounding.
- Identify the procedure and inputs needed to reproduce a calculation.
- Calculate a recruitment target allowing for expected missing outcomes.
- Assess recruitment feasibility using a screening and enrollment funnel.

:::

You can now apply these ideas to two-arm treatment comparisons. The formulas below assume two [independent groups](#independent-groups) with equal allocation and a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test). Studies that randomize hospitals, compare body sites within participants, or collect repeated measurements require calculations that account for dependence; see [units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis). The [recruitment section below](#account-for-expected-losses) considers whether you can obtain enough usable outcomes; the [reporting chapter](#reporting) brings the calculation and its justification together.

Having specified the chronic pain target difference and acceptable error risks, you can calculate the required number of analyzable patients. The first calculation concerns that trial; the next concerns a continuous-outcome comparison. You can then allow for missing outcomes and assess how long recruitment would take.

## How error probabilities and power affect sample size {#how-error-rates-and-power-affect-sample-size .core-heading}

Your sample size calculation needs to account for two choices: the acceptable Type I error probability and the target power. A lower Type I error probability requires stronger evidence before concluding that the treatments differ. Higher power means a greater probability of detecting the target difference if it is the true population difference. In this calculation, lowering the Type I error probability or increasing target power increases the unrounded sample size requirement, with the other inputs unchanged.

For the normal approximation, these choices are translated into [$z$-values](#z-value): positions on the standard normal bell-shaped curve, centered at zero with a standard deviation of one. They are then combined into a sample size multiplier, $M$:

\begin{equation}
M=\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}\right)^2.
(\#eq:multiplier)
\end{equation}

Here, $\alpha$ is the Type I error probability, $\beta$ is the [Type II error probability](#beta), and $1-\beta$ is the target power.

A $z$-value describes how many standard deviations a position lies from the center of that curve. Its subscript gives the proportion of the distribution below that position. For example, $z_{0.975}=1.96$ means that 97.5% of the distribution lies below 1.96. This position is called a [quantile](#quantile).

For a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%:

- The 5% error allowance is split between the two ends of the distribution: 2.5% in each tail. This gives $z_{1-0.05/2}=z_{0.975}\approx1.96$.
- The target power of 90% gives $z_{0.90}\approx1.28$.
- The multiplier is therefore approximately $(1.96+1.28)^2\approx10.51$, using the unrounded $z$-values.

Figure \@ref(fig:normal-multiplier) shows what these distances mean for a treatment comparison. The upper curve applies when the population difference is zero; the lower applies when it equals the target difference. The same rejection boundaries apply in both cases. Separating the centers by about 1.96 + 1.28 standard errors puts about 90% of the lower curve beyond the upper boundary.

This multiplier combines the chosen error probabilities and power. The sample size calculation also uses the target difference and variability. You can use the table below without calculating the $z$-values yourself. The appropriate calculation still depends on your study design and planned analysis [@kirkwood2003; @wang2020].

```{r multiplier}
# Probabilities are entered as decimals: .05 = 5%, .90 = 90%.
alpha <- .05
target_power <- .90
# qnorm() finds standard-normal cutoffs. Divide alpha by 2 for two tails.
# Add the cutoffs, then square the sum (^2) to obtain the multiplier M.
M <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(target_power))^2
M
```

```{r normal-multiplier, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=6, fig.cap="The two curves represent different population scenarios. Above: no treatment difference (H0 true), with 5% in the two rejection tails. Below: the target difference (H0 false), with approximately 90% beyond the upper rejection boundary. On the standard-error scale, 1.96 plus 1.28 separates the two centers; squaring this distance gives M = 10.51.", fig.alt="Two sampling distributions on the same standard-error scale. The upper distribution is centered at zero under H0; the lower is centered at the target difference, 3.24 standard errors above zero. The same rejection boundaries are used for both. Shading shows false positives under H0 and power at the target difference."}
draw_normal_multiplier()
```

```{r multiplier-table, echo=FALSE}
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(.05, .01), power = c(.80, .90, .95))
grid$multiplier <- with(grid, (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power))^2)
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(grid, c("alpha", "power")), digits = 2,
  caption = "Normal-approximation sample-size multipliers for different Type I error probability and target-power choices.")
```

The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) identifies the procedures used here and explains what should accompany an exported calculation.

## Two proportions {.core-heading}

The event percentages in each group and the target difference between them are your starting inputs. For the chronic pain trial, the calculation assumes 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment: a target difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

For two independent groups of equal size and a two-sided test, the tutorial and apps use the normal approximation in R's `power.prop.test()` [@rcore]. You specify the two event probabilities, Type I error probability and target power. The result is the required analyzable number per group, before allowing for losses.

```{r proportions}
# Relief probabilities for novel treatment (t) and standard treatment (c).
pi_t <- .60
pi_c <- .30
# With n omitted, R finds patients per group for the requested power.
# two.sided allows either direction; strict = TRUE counts both rejection tails.
pain_plan <- power.prop.test(p1 = pi_t, p2 = pi_c,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n selects the calculated count. ceiling() rounds upward to a whole patient.
n_raw <- pain_plan$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_raw)
# Retain this count for the later recruitment example.
pain_lab_n <- n_per_group
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r proportions-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the chronic pain trial using the normal planning approximation.")
```

The unrounded result is `r round(n_raw, 2)` patients per group. Rounding upward gives `r n_per_group` per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. This is the count used in the recruitment and fixed-sample sensitivity examples below. The `strict = TRUE` setting counts significant results in either direction for the two-sided test.

The calculation targets 90% power under the stated assumptions. Actual power for the planned test can differ because the calculation is approximate; simulation lets you examine that performance. Your report should identify the method, assumptions and rounding, and account for expected losses separately.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-definitive-sample">
<summary>Common misconception: the calculator provides one definitive minimum number</summary>

The calculated sample size depends on the effect, event probabilities or variability, error targets and analysis method you specify. It is a conditional planning result. You should check plausible alternative assumptions and whether the reported number is per group or for the whole study before interpreting it.

</details>

```{r proportion-changes}
# Each row specifies a different set of assumptions.
proportion_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Smaller difference", "Lower probabilities",
               "Type I error probability 1%", "Power 95%"),
  treatment = c(.60, .60, .30, .60, .60),
  control = c(.30, .45, .15, .30, .30),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
# mapply() calculates a sample size for each row using its four inputs.
proportion_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_proportions,
  proportion_cases$treatment, proportion_cases$control,
  proportion_cases$alpha, proportion_cases$power)
proportion_cases$total <- 2 * proportion_cases$per_group
# Convert probabilities to percentages for display; calculations use decimals.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(proportion_cases,
  c("treatment", "control", "alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative binary-outcome assumptions, using the same normal planning approximation as the tutorial and apps.")
```

For a yes/no outcome, the calculation uses the event percentage in each group. For example, 30% versus 15% and 60% versus 45% both differ by 15 percentage points, but they need not require the same sample size. The amount of [sampling variability](#sampling-variability) also depends on where those percentages lie. Halving the difference therefore does not necessarily multiply the required sample size by exactly four. The table lets you compare these assumptions directly.

Read a row as a conditional statement: if those event probabilities and that analysis are reasonable, then this is the approximate number required for the specified error targets. The smaller-difference row needs more participants because sampling variability makes that difference harder to distinguish from zero.

In the [two-proportion app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_proportions/), you can compare the sample sizes needed at different power targets.

<div id="calculate-sample-size">

```{r calculation-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_calculation", "Calculate the chronic pain trial's analyzable requirement, then use the recruitment section below to allow for unavailable outcomes.")
```

</div>

At a 20-percentage-point target difference (50% versus 30%), the same procedure requires `r report_example$facts$sensitivity_n` analyzable patients per group for 90% power, compared with `r report_example$facts$analyzable` at 30 points. This quantifies the decision introduced in Chapter 1: detecting the smaller worthwhile difference with the same power requires more patients.

<details id="adherence" class="optional-practice">
<summary>Additional practice: preventing gestational diabetes</summary>

Suppose you want to find out whether probiotic supplementation prevents gestational diabetes in pregnant women with overweight or obesity (BMI at least 25 kg/m²). Randomly allocate women to probiotics or no probiotics, with otherwise comparable care, and assess gestational diabetes using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Your plan should specify the supplement, diagnostic criteria and assessment time before planning. An assessment at 20–24 weeks needs justification against applicable clinical guidance: NICE generally recommends risk-based testing at 24–28 weeks [@nicegdm]. For an observational study of supplementation, confounding requires an appropriate analysis and planning method.

For this calculation, assume gestational diabetes occurs in 20% without probiotics and 10% with probiotics. The target reduction is 10 percentage points. The task is to express the outcome consistently when entering these percentages.

The same planning assumption can be expressed using either developing the disease or remaining free of it:

| Outcome entered | Without probiotics | With probiotics |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Develops gestational diabetes | 20% | 10% |
| Remains free of gestational diabetes | 80% | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:gdm-outcome-direction) Two ways to express the same assumed effect of probiotics.

The [probiotics calculation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=probiotics_calculation) uses the second row. A 10-percentage-point increase in remaining disease-free represents the same comparison as a 10-percentage-point reduction in developing the disease. Your report should identify the event entered.

```{r adherence-case}
# Load the same example inputs used by the app.
adherence_case <- teaching_case("adherence")
adherence_plan <- teaching_case_spec("adherence")
# Calculate patients per group for the example's target power.
adherence_plan$n <- plan_n(adherence_plan, "testing",
  adherence_case$inputs$target_power)
# Display the analyzable count in each group and across both groups.
c(analyzable_per_group = adherence_plan$n,
  analyzable_total = 2 * adherence_plan$n,
  planning_power = spec_power(adherence_plan))
```

```{r adherence-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=adherence_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*adherence_plan$n, `Planning power`=percent(spec_power(adherence_plan)),check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the hypothetical gestational-diabetes prevention trial.")
```

```{r probiotics-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("probiotics_calculation", "Apply the calculation to a prevention trial, recording which event the percentages describe.")
```

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Advanced: simulate the prevention trial</summary>

The [probiotics simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence) also considers a recruitment ceiling of 240 and 15% unavailable outcomes. These assumptions give a requirement of `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n, adherence_case$inputs$dropout)` recruits. The [advanced feasibility discussion](#stress-test-the-study-plan) explains how to assess such a shortfall.

</details>

</details>

## Two means {.core-heading}

For a continuous outcome, you should identify the target difference and the [standard deviation](#standard-deviation) in the same measurement units before calculating.

In the formula below, $n$ is the number of patients needed in each group, $\delta$ is the target difference between the group means, and $\sigma$ is the assumed SD of individual scores within each group. The calculation assumes the same SD in both groups. The multiplier $M$ combines the error-probability and power choices explained above:

\begin{equation}
n\approx M\frac{2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}.
(\#eq:means)
\end{equation}

Suppose an earlier study observed a 4-unit [between-group difference](#expected-difference) in a normally distributed improvement score. The calculation uses a target difference of 3 units and an SD of 5 units in both groups. Patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically important. The example uses a hypothetical, approximately normally distributed improvement score. The Type I error probability is 5% and target power is 90%.

The normal formula makes the calculation transparent:

\[
n\approx10.51\times\frac{2\times5^2}{3^2}\approx58.4.
\]

```{r means}
# Target mean difference and common standard deviation, in score units.
delta <- 3
sigma <- 5
# The normal formula illustrates how the inputs affect the requirement.
# The factor 2 allows for variability in both independent groups.
normal_n_raw <- M * 2 * sigma^2 / delta^2
c(unrounded_per_group = normal_n_raw,
  rounded_per_group = ceiling(normal_n_raw))
```

The normal approximation gives 58.4 patients per group, which rounds upward to 59. The planned analysis is a pooled two-sample t-test, which accounts for estimating the common SD from the trial data. Its sample size calculation gives 60 patients per group. The app and subsequent examples use this result.

```{r t-test-planning}
# Plan the pooled two-sample t test with the same inputs.
# strict = TRUE includes rejection in either direction.
t_plan <- power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)
# Round upward within each group, then add the two groups.
n_per_group <- ceiling(t_plan$n)
t_plan
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r means-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the continuous-outcome comparison, planned for a pooled two-sample t test.")
```

The result is `r n_per_group` analyzable patients per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. The recruitment section below allows for expected missing outcomes. Smaller target differences require larger samples because they are harder to distinguish from patient-to-patient variation. In the normal formula, halving the difference or doubling the SD multiplies the unrounded requirement by four. The t-test calculation gives approximately this increase.

<details>
<summary>Raw and standardized differences</summary>

The target difference of 3 score units is a raw between-group difference. Dividing it by the common SD gives the standardized difference: $d=3/5=0.60$. If the SD were 10 units, the same 3-unit difference would give $d=0.30$. The clinical difference is unchanged, but it is smaller relative to patient-to-patient variation and requires more patients to detect. A standardized effect is therefore not, by itself, a measure of clinical importance. Keeping the difference in the outcome's original units helps you explain what it would mean clinically; standardized measures can help compare results across scales [@kallogjeri2023].

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where does the assumed SD come from?</summary>

Previous studies can inform the SD, but their patients, measurement scale, follow-up time and analysis should be relevant to your study. The SD of change from baseline is not interchangeable with the SD of final scores. A review of knee osteoarthritis trials found substantial variation in pain-score variability across studies [@bentin2026]. Its estimates concern continuous WOMAC pain scores. The binary pain-relief example requires assumptions about event percentages.

Your study plan should document the source of the assumed SD and examine a plausible range using the [two-means app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_means/).

</details>

Your study plan should record the inputs, pooled two-sample t-test procedure, software, two-sided test, equal allocation, and rounded counts. The advanced [software and statistical support guide](#software-support) reviews calculation software and explains when early advice from a statistician is useful. Its [worked example](#gpower-assumptions) shows how an effect-size input can change the result.

<details id="rehabilitation" class="optional-practice">
<summary>Additional practice: rehabilitation</summary>

For additional practice, consider six-week mobility improvement in two independent rehabilitation groups. The calculation above used a target difference of 3 score units and a common SD of 5. How would the required sample change if relevant evidence instead supported an SD of 7, with the other inputs unchanged?

```{r rehabilitation-case}
# Load the rehabilitation example shared with the app.
rehabilitation_case <- teaching_case("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan <- teaching_case_spec("rehabilitation")
# Calculate patients per group from the difference, SD, error probability and power.
rehabilitation_plan$n <- sample_size_two_means(
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_delta, rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_sd,
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$alpha, rehabilitation_case$inputs$target_power)
# Report the analyzable requirement before the recruitment adjustment in Chapter 2.
c(analyzable_per_group = rehabilitation_plan$n,
  total = 2 * rehabilitation_plan$n)
```

```{r rehabilitation-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=rehabilitation_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*rehabilitation_plan$n, check.names=FALSE), caption="Analyzable sample size for the rehabilitation comparison.")
```

<details id="rehabilitation-report">
<summary>Example report for the mean-score comparison</summary>

The trial compares mean six-week mobility improvement between two equally sized, independent rehabilitation groups using a pooled two-sample t test. A target difference of 3 score units, common SD of 5, two-sided Type I error probability of 5%, and 90% power require `r rehabilitation_plan$n` analyzable patients per group. Allowing for 5% unavailable outcomes gives `r ceiling(rehabilitation_plan$n / .95)` recruits per group (`r 2 * ceiling(rehabilitation_plan$n / .95)` total). The calculation uses R `r report_example$r_version`, stats `r report_example$stats_version`, and `power.t.test()` with `type = "two.sample"`, `alternative = "two.sided"` and `strict = TRUE`.

</details>

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-rehabilitation-sd">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The pooled t-test calculation increases from `r rehabilitation_plan$n` to `r sample_size_two_means(3, 7, .05, .90)` analyzable patients per group. The larger SD represents more variation between patients, so more observations are needed to distinguish the same 3-unit difference. The evidence supporting the selected SD belongs in the report.

</details>

Although an improvement score uses before/after information within each patient, this example analyzes one score per patient across two independent groups. A single-group paired comparison, repeated-measures model, or baseline-adjusted analysis needs its own planning method.

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Advanced: simulate rehabilitation outcomes</summary>

The [rehabilitation simulation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation) uses a t-test planning method. *One study* generates independent, normally distributed improvement scores. Its test evaluates evidence against a zero population difference. *Many studies* shows how conclusions vary under the same population assumptions. This optional advanced extension can be used after the core calculation.

</details>

```{r rehabilitation-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("rehabilitation_calculation", "Compare SDs of 5 and 7 for a target difference of 3 units, keeping power, error probability and allocation unchanged.")
```

</details>

The following sections use the analyzable count to calculate recruitment and assess feasibility. Your record should identify the inputs, method, and analyzable count per group and in total. The [discharge exercise](#discharge) offers further optional calculation practice.

<span id="feasibility"></span>

## Allowing for expected missing outcomes {#account-for-expected-losses .core-heading}

The calculation gives patients needed for analysis. The recruitment target also allows for patients whose four-week outcome will be unavailable.


If some recruited patients are expected to have no usable outcome, you will need to recruit more patients than the calculation requires for analysis. Here, $n$ is the required number per group and $r$ is the expected proportion lost, so $1-r$ is the expected [retention proportion](#retention). The brackets mean "round upward to the next whole patient":

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{recruit,arm}}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{1-r}\right\rceil.
(\#eq:dropout)
\end{equation}

The expected loss should draw on studies or records with a comparable population, treatment, outcome and follow-up period. For example, if 20 of 200 enrolled patients in a comparable study lacked the required outcome, the observed loss was 20/200 = 10%. Using $r=0.10$ in a new study assumes that this experience is relevant. Reasons for missing outcomes, differences between arms and uncertainty in a small pilot should inform that judgment. When evidence is limited, your report should identify a plausible range and show how recruitment changes across it.

```{r recruitment}
# Start with the 56 patients per group needed for analysis.
analyzable_per_group <- pain_lab_n
# Divide by the expected retained fraction, 95%, then round upward.
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / (1 - .05))
c(analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group, recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

```{r recruitment-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=analyzable_per_group, `Recruit per group`=recruit_per_group, `Recruit total`=2*recruit_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Chronic-pain recruitment target allowing for 5% expected loss.")
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout-arithmetic">
<summary>Common misconception: allowing for 10% dropout means adding 10%</summary>

If you expect 10% of participants to be lost, approximately 90% will remain. You should therefore divide the required analyzable sample size by 0.90. For example, 100 analyzable participants require recruiting 112 participants after rounding up.

</details>

For the chronic pain trial, 5% expected loss means approximately 95% of recruits will contribute to the analysis. To obtain `r analyzable_per_group` patients per group with usable outcomes, you would plan to recruit `r analyzable_per_group`/0.95 = `r round(analyzable_per_group / .95, 2)`, rounded upward to `r recruit_per_group` per group.

<span id="model-answer-protocol-counts"></span>
The protocol should report both the required [analyzable sample](#analyzable-sample-size) and the recruitment target, per group and in total: here, `r 2 * analyzable_per_group` analyzable patients and `r 2 * recruit_per_group` recruits across the two groups.

Missing outcomes may be more common in one treatment group or among patients with poor outcomes. Your study should plan for follow-up and an appropriate analysis as well as the expected count. The advanced [missing-outcome extension](#explore-missing-outcomes) examines unequal losses and possible bias.


```{r recruitment-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("recruitment", "Use your analyzable count and one expected loss percentage to calculate recruitment per group and in total.")
```


<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout">
<summary>Common misconception: recruiting extra participants resolves missing-data problems</summary>

Recruiting extra participants can help preserve the analyzable sample size and statistical power. Addressing missing-data bias requires prevention, appropriate analysis, and sensitivity analyses alongside the recruitment allowance [@little2012missing].

</details>

Treatment discontinuation, switching and rescue medication can affect the treatment difference used in planning. The advanced section [Treatment changes and the outcome you want to compare](#treatment-changes) explains how these events enter the research question and calculation.

## Assessing recruitment feasibility {#recruitment-feasibility .core-heading}

The recruitment target should be compared with the number of patients the clinics can enroll within the available time. Screening records help distinguish patients seen in routine care from those who meet the study criteria, can participate and agree to enroll.

For example, the clinics see 100 potentially relevant patients each month. Of these, 40 are eligible and 30 remain available after allowing for competing studies and practical barriers. If half of those 30 consent, expected recruitment is 15 participants per month. Each step uses the patients remaining after the previous step.

```{r recruitment-funnel, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Monthly recruitment funnel for the chronic pain trial. Each stage is conditional on the preceding stage: 100 potentially relevant patients, 40 eligible, 30 available, and 15 enrolled. Counts refer to distinct patients.", fig.alt="A narrowing funnel shows 100 potentially relevant patients per month, then 40 meeting eligibility criteria, 30 available after competing studies and practical barriers, and 15 consenting and enrolling. Half of the 30 available patients consent."}
draw_recruitment_funnel()
```

At this rate, recruiting `r 2 * recruit_per_group` patients would take `r ceiling(2 * recruit_per_group / 15)` whole months. The supporting plan should also consider site-opening delays and a slower recruitment scenario. The advanced section [Exploring power and uncertain assumptions](#planning-uncertainty) examines the evidence behind recruitment forecasts, while [Options when the study provides insufficient information](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose) discusses changes to the design or recruitment plan.

<details class="misconception" id="lasagnas-law">
<summary>Common misconception: many patients in the clinic means enough recruits</summary>

*Lasagna's law* describes the tendency to overestimate how many patients will actually be available for a study. Eligibility criteria, willingness to participate, competing studies and practical barriers reduce the pool. A recruitment forecast should follow these steps using recent screening and enrollment records [@lasagna1979].

</details>

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Two-group calculations depend on the target difference, variability or event probabilities, Type I error probability and power.
- The result should identify analyzable participants per group and in total.
- Recruitment allows for expected missing outcomes, with rounding upward within each group.
- Screening and enrollment records help assess whether the recruitment target is feasible.
- The [reporting chapter](#reporting) brings the method, inputs, software and rounding together.

</div>

# The sample size calculation report {#reporting .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Identify the essential elements in a worked sample size calculation report.
- Evaluate whether its assumptions, analysis and participant counts agree.
- Correct incomplete or inconsistent reporting.
- Write a concise calculation report with traceable inputs, software and supporting reasoning.
:::

A useful report lets another researcher understand your decisions and reproduce the calculation. The concise calculation report presents the selected design and numerical result; the supporting study plan retains evidence, alternative assumptions and unresolved decisions. The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) creates both from one set of answers.

## A complete sample size calculation report {#write-a-sample-size-justification .core-heading}

Example 3.1 brings together the decisions developed in Chapters 1 and 2. Blue annotations identify the information another researcher needs to understand and repeat the calculation.

The example and checklist follow PICO, SPIRIT 2025, CONSORT 2025, DELTA² and section 4.1 of the UMCG SAP template [@richardson1995; @spiritconsort2025; @consortee2025; @cook2018delta2; @umcgsap; @roa2024comet]. UMCG students and researchers can access the [SAP template in Zenya](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78).

<div class="annotated-report" role="group" aria-labelledby="sample-size-report-caption">
<p class="caption" id="sample-size-report-caption"><span id="sample-size-calculation-report">Example 3.1: Sample size calculation report for the chronic pain trial.</span></p>

<p class="report-part">Question and design</p>

The trial will <span class="report-mark">[A] individually randomize adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, bilateral lower-extremity pain due to diabetic peripheral neuropathy for at least one year, and BMI ≥18 and <40 kg/m² to Neravixa or duloxetine in a 1:1 ratio. The primary outcome is achieved pain relief at four weeks, recorded as yes or no</span> using the same prespecified question in both groups. The treatment effect is the absolute difference in relief percentages, Neravixa minus duloxetine.

<p class="report-part">Assumptions and evidence</p>

The pilot observed relief in 7 of 10 patients receiving novel treatment and 3 of 10 receiving standard treatment. Given the uncertainty of these small-sample estimates, the calculation uses <span class="report-mark">[B] 60% relief with novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, a target difference of 30 percentage points</span>, below the pilot's 40-point difference. Patient and clinical advisers set the minimum worthwhile increase at 20 percentage points: one additional patient reporting relief per five treated with the novel treatment instead of standard treatment. They judged this additional relief necessary to justify four additional safety-monitoring visits and the risk of short-lived dizziness.

<p class="report-part">Calculation</p>

The primary comparison will use a <span class="report-mark">[C] two-sided pooled score test for independent proportions without continuity correction or covariate adjustment</span>. A normal planning approximation with <span class="report-mark">[D] a Type I error probability of 5% and 90% power at the 30-point target difference</span> gives <span class="report-mark">[E] `r sprintf("%.2f", report_example$facts$raw_n)` analyzable patients per group, rounded upward to `r report_example$facts$analyzable` per group (`r 2 * report_example$facts$analyzable` total)</span>. The conventional two-sided 5% significance level is used; the 90% power target limits the probability of failing to detect the target difference to 10%. The calculation uses <span class="report-mark">[F] R `r report_example$r_version`, stats `r report_example$stats_version`, and `stats::power.prop.test()` with `alternative = "two.sided"` and `strict = TRUE`</span>.

<p class="report-part">Recruitment</p>

Given the short four-week assessment period, the calculation allows for <span class="report-mark">[E] 5% unavailable primary outcomes in each group. Dividing the analyzable requirement by 0.95 gives `r report_example$facts$recruitment` recruits per group: `r report_example$facts$analyzable`/0.95, rounded upward, or `r 2 * report_example$facts$recruitment` participants in total</span>.

</div>

| Label | What this part makes explicit |
|:--|:--|
| A: Question and design | Population, primary outcome, time point and allocation. |
| B: Numerical assumptions | Both event percentages, the target difference and the reasoning behind the selected values. |
| C: Procedure | The planned test, sidedness, corrections and covariate adjustment. |
| D: Statistical performance | Type I error probability and power at the specified difference. |
| E: Participant counts | Unrounded and rounded requirements, per-group and total counts, and the loss allowance. |
| F: Software | Function, settings and versions needed to repeat the calculation. |

Table: (\#tab:report-annotations) Essential elements of the sample size calculation report in Example 3.1. Letters connect the explanation to the blue annotations.

The accompanying [R code and software record](#sample-size-report-methods) reproduce the calculation: `r report_example$facts$analyzable` analyzable patients per group, followed by the 5% loss adjustment to `r report_example$facts$recruitment` recruits per group.

<details class="report-methods" id="sample-size-report-methods">
<summary>Calculation procedure and software record</summary>

This calculation uses R `r report_example$r_version` and stats `r report_example$stats_version`. `stats::` identifies the package supplying `power.prop.test()`. Setting `strict = TRUE` includes rejection in either direction of the two-sided test. The [methods record](#tutorial-methods) explains the analysis and confidence interval used in the simulation app.

```{r report-command}
# Calculate patients per group for the specified event probabilities and power.
plan <- stats::power.prop.test(
  p1 = 0.60, p2 = 0.30, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n extracts the calculated count; ceiling() rounds it upward to a whole patient.
analyzable_per_group <- ceiling(plan$n)
# Allow for 5% unavailable outcomes, rounding within each group.
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / 0.95)
# c() collects the named results to display together.
c(unrounded_per_group = plan$n,
  analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  analyzable_total = 2 * analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group,
  recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) includes the prepared calculation's software record when the chronic pain comparison is selected. An attached calculator result retains the inputs and software used for that result. The [reproducibility chapter](#reproducibility-record) explains the full record.

</details>

## What belongs in the report? {#record-assumptions .core-heading}

Table \@ref(tab:planning-assumptions) uses the same four headings as the report activity. The linked chapters explain each decision. The advanced view develops evidence appraisal, alternative assumptions and feasibility in more detail.

::: {.planning-assumptions}

| Decision | What to make explicit |
|---|---|
| **Question and design** | [Chapter 1: Research question and power](#clinical-question) introduces this section. |
| Research question: PICO | Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome, including the measurement time point |
| Intervention and comparator | What each group receives, how it is delivered, by whom and on what schedule; relevant dose or intensity and permitted additional care |
| Design, sampling and allocation | Study design, participant selection, unit of allocation and allocation ratio; any paired, repeated or clustered observations |
| **Assumptions and evidence** | [Chapter 1](#clinical-question) develops the assumptions; [Exploring power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) examines alternatives. |
| Effect scale | Treatment minus control; score units or percentage points; direction of benefit |
| Difference observed in previous data | Observed result, source, relevance and uncertainty; gaps in the available evidence |
| Clinical threshold | Smallest worthwhile between-group benefit, justified against treatment harms, burden and alternatives |
| Target difference | Difference used in the power calculation, with justification |
| Variation or event probabilities | Common standard deviation or both groups' event percentages; source, population, outcome definition and assessment time |
| Evidence relevance and uncertainty | Whether differences in patients, care or measurement limit applicability; uncertain inputs and evidence needed |
| Sensitivity analysis | Plausible alternatives supported by the evidence review; whether sample size changes or stays fixed, and implications for the recommendation |
| **Calculation** | [Chapter 1: Research question and power](#power) explains the criteria; [Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment](#calculations) supplies the calculations. |
| Planned analysis | Planned test and sidedness; how pairing or clustering will be handled, where relevant |
| Calculation procedure and software | Method or formula; software, package and code versions; saved inputs and calculation steps. For simulations: data-generating assumptions, repetitions and random-number settings. See [Methods and software to record](#reproducibility-record) |
| Type I error probability and target power | Chosen probabilities and the target difference at which power is evaluated |
| Sample size needed or available for analysis | Per-group and total analyzable counts; calculation result and upward rounding, or the available sample for an existing-data study |
| **Recruitment and conclusion** | [Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment](#calculations) connects the analyzable count to a recruitment target and final justification. |
| Losses, missing data and recruitment | Expected losses, recruitment target and how missing outcomes or treatment changes affect the plan |
| Feasibility and resources | Expected recruitment rate, recruitment period, available resources and other practical constraints |
| Intended conclusion | What the design could establish and what remains uncertain |

Table: (\#tab:planning-assumptions) Decisions and assumptions to record in the study-plan activity, with links to the core chapters that develop each part of the study plan.

:::

@wang2024bep illustrate how evidence supports numerical inputs, using local data for the control percentage and a systematic review for the target risk ratio. Your supporting plan should retain each source, its relevance and the plausible alternatives considered; [Chapter 5](#planning-uncertainty) develops that assessment.

Clear reporting also makes measurement choices open to scrutiny. In a review of 185 studies using the BREAST-Q Reconstruction Module, a patient-reported questionnaire for breast reconstruction, only 17 reported a sample-size calculation and 71 reported the primary outcome's assessment time; 36 had questionnaire-administration errors [@gallo2022]. These findings underline why your plan should specify how and when the outcome is measured alongside the calculation. Missing calculation details leave the sample-size justification unassessable. A review of 385 phase III oncology trials found that 41 (10.6%) cited previous clinical data to support the assumed hazard ratio. This concerns the evidence behind the numerical assumption, reinforcing the need to report both the calculation and the sources supporting its inputs [@noticewala2025effects].

<span id="report-statistical-criteria"></span>
<span id="report-calculation-method"></span>

The [optional mean-score report](#rehabilitation-report) gives the corresponding t-test example. [Estimation reporting](#estimation-report) uses a confidence level and precision target. Designs with several outcomes or interim decisions need the [additional design record](#complex-design-record).

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- The report should state what was calculated, why those inputs were chosen, and how the result can be reproduced.
