# Sample size for estimation {#estimation-planning .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Distinguish an estimate from the population quantity it describes.
- Explain confidence level, interval width and the repeated-study meaning of a confidence interval.
- Plan a sample size for a desired precision and interpret the interval clinically.
- Write an estimation-based sample size calculation report with a justified precision target.
- Assess the precision available from an existing dataset or a pilot study.
:::

Suppose you are planning a neuropathy care service for adults with type 2 diabetes attending a diabetes clinic. How many of these patients have peripheral neuropathy? An estimate of that percentage would help the clinic anticipate its follow-up workload. Each sampled patient is assessed once, at enrollment.

A recent clinic study planned its neuropathy prevalence estimate using a 95% confidence level, an anticipated prevalence of 22%, and a five-percentage-point margin of error [@negussie2024]. The worked service plan below follows this approach using a planning assumption of 20%: about one patient in five. The aim is a 95% confidence interval roughly five percentage points either side of the estimate. Later sections consider a population mean, treatment differences, existing data and pilot retention.

## Estimates, confidence intervals and precision {#estimation-foundations .advanced-heading}

A sample estimate changes when different participants are sampled. A [confidence interval](#confidence-interval){.no-glossary-tooltip} uses the data and analysis assumptions to give a range describing uncertainty about the population quantity. A narrower interval indicates greater [precision](#precision){.no-glossary-tooltip}. Across repeated studies, about 95% of intervals calculated by a 95% confidence-interval method contain the true population value under its assumptions.

Figure \@ref(fig:twenty-prevalence-intervals) shows one illustrative batch of 20 surveys. The population prevalence is fixed at 20%; the sample estimates and their intervals change between surveys. The green intervals contain 20%, while the red interval misses it.

```{r twenty-prevalence-intervals, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="Twenty illustrative surveys of 246 adults, with population neuropathy prevalence fixed at 20%. Nineteen green intervals contain 20%; one red interval misses it. Circles and a cross distinguish the two outcomes as well as color. This batch illustrates the repeated-study meaning of 95% confidence.", fig.alt="Twenty horizontal confidence intervals around survey estimates. A vertical line marks population neuropathy prevalence of 20%. Nineteen green intervals cross the line; one red interval, marked by a cross, lies entirely below it."}
draw_prevalence_coverage()
```

For example, a population percentage estimated as 20% with an interval from 15% to 25% has a full width of 10 percentage points and a margin of 5 points on either side. The [full width](#full-width) and confidence level should be chosen for the decision the estimate will inform. Under the same planning model, higher confidence or a narrower target width increases the unrounded sample size requirement.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-confidence-probability">
<summary>Common misconception: this interval has a 95% probability of containing the population percentage</summary>

The true population percentage is fixed, while the interval changes from sample to sample. The 95% describes how often the method produces an interval containing that percentage across repeated studies.

</details>

The clinic survey starts with a desired margin of error. The next section turns that precision target into a total sample size.

## Estimate one proportion: a prevalence survey {#prevalence .advanced-heading}

A prevalence survey estimates one population proportion at a defined time. Each participant contributes a binary outcome to one sample; you choose its size for a useful [margin of error](#margin-of-error).

Such estimates can inform service planning or recruitment and retention assumptions for a future trial. The planning question is how precisely the study should estimate the population percentage [@pourhoseingholi2013; @ying2025].

For the neuropathy service plan, the desired margin of error is 5 [percentage points](#percentage-points): half-width $d=0.05$, or a full width of 10 points, at 95% confidence. Here, n is the total number of independently sampled patients from the clinic register.

For an anticipated population proportion $p_0$, the normal approximation gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^{2}p_0(1-p_0)}{d^2}.
(\#eq:single-proportion)
\end{equation}

Here $p_0$ is the anticipated population proportion used to plan the study. If comparable evidence suggests a prevalence of 20% ($p_0=0.20$), the approximate requirement is 246 completed observations. If there is no useful prior estimate, 50% ($p_0=0.50$) gives the largest value of $p_0(1-p_0)$ and an approximate requirement of 385.

```{r single-proportion-precision}
# Plan for a full width of 10 percentage points at 95% confidence.
prevalence_known <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95)
# unknown_p = TRUE uses 50%, the conservative value for this approximation.
prevalence_unknown <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95, unknown_p = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Prior estimate 20%", "Unknown: use 50% for planning"),
  `Assumed population percentage` = percent(c(prevalence_known$planning_p,
    prevalence_unknown$planning_p)),
  `Completed observations` = c(prevalence_known$n, prevalence_unknown$n),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate prevalence sample sizes for a 95% interval with a 5-percentage-point margin of error.")
```

The conservative 50% choice concerns absolute precision for one proportion under this approximation. For a rare outcome, an absolute margin of five percentage points might be unhelpfully wide; event counts and the chosen interval method also matter.

Reducing the margin of error from 5 to 2.5 percentage points requires about four times as many completed assessments under this formula. The app below applies these choices to the neuropathy survey and shows an interval from a simulated sample.

```{r prevalence-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("prevalence", "Compare sample sizes and confidence interval widths for one population percentage.")
```

These survey decisions can now be brought together in a sample size calculation report.

## Reporting an estimation-based sample size {#estimation-report .advanced-heading}

An estimation plan identifies the population quantity, outcome and assessment time, confidence level, desired full interval width, anticipated percentages or SD, interval method, software and participant counts. Its justification explains why the chosen width would be useful. For existing data, it describes the available count and anticipated precision. The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) displays these fields when an estimation goal is selected; [Chapter 3](#reporting) explains the common report structure.

The report below follows the study-size and statistical-method reporting items in STROBE and the precision-based approach in the published neuropathy study [@strobe2007; @negussie2024]. The selected margin corresponds to uncertainty of about five affected patients per 100 clinic patients, which is the tolerance used for the service's initial workload plan.

<div class="annotated-report" id="estimation-report-example" role="group" aria-labelledby="estimation-report-caption">

<p class="caption" id="estimation-report-caption">Example 4.1. Sample size calculation report for the neuropathy prevalence survey.</p>

Peripheral neuropathy prevalence will be estimated among adults with type 2 diabetes attending the clinic, using one assessment per patient at enrollment. Patients will be selected by simple random sampling from the clinic register. With anticipated prevalence of 20%, 95% confidence and a margin of error of five percentage points, the single-proportion normal approximation gives $1.96^2\times0.20\times0.80/0.05^2=245.86$, rounded upward to 246 completed assessments. The margin was chosen to support workload planning to within approximately five affected patients per 100 clinic patients. Allowing for 5% nonresponse gives $\lceil246/0.95\rceil=259$ patients to approach. The observed prevalence will be reported with a 95% Wilson confidence interval. The calculation uses R `r getRversion()`, `stats::qnorm(0.975)` and the formula shown; the interval uses the Wilson score method without continuity correction. The inputs and commented code are retained with the calculation record.

</div>

The following draft concerns the same survey. Its highlighted passages can be selected to inspect the calculation and reporting problems.

```{r estimation-report-error, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("estimation_report")
```

## Estimating a population mean {#plan-for-precision .advanced-heading}

The same precision-based approach can be used for a population mean, with the SD describing variability between patients.

A rehabilitation study aims to estimate the mean improvement in one patient population. You should specify how narrow the confidence interval needs to be to support a useful interpretation. Here, a 95% confidence interval with an anticipated full width of 4 score units is the precision target [@wang2020; @lakens2022].

With an assumed SD of 5 units, the [mean estimation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision) finds the smallest total sample meeting this target. The calculation uses the confidence level, SD and desired width. The population mean used in simulation is 3 units, which supplies a known value for checking the intervals.

```{r precision-plan}
# Define one population and the desired precision for its mean.
# The mean of 3 supplies a known value for checking interval coverage.
precision_spec <- single_population_spec(outcome = "means", mean = 3,
  sd = 5, confidence = .95, width = 4, B = 5000, seed = 20260922)
# Find the smallest total sample meeting the expected interval-width target.
precision_n <- single_population_n(precision_spec)
c(analyzable_total = precision_n,
  anticipated_full_width = single_population_width(precision_spec, precision_n))
# Repeated samples produce different estimates and interval widths.
precision_batch <- single_population_simulate(precision_spec, precision_n, many = TRUE)
```

```{r precision-plan-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable participants (total)`=precision_n, `Anticipated full interval width`=round(single_population_width(precision_spec, precision_n),2),check.names=FALSE), caption="Total sample required to estimate one population mean with a 95% confidence interval of anticipated full width at most 4 score units, assuming SD 5.")
```

For normal data, this calculation uses the expected full width of a t-based interval. Realized interval widths vary with the sample SD. The simulation shows how often intervals contain the known population mean and how often their width meets the chosen target [@sandoval2025].

```{r precision-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("mean_precision", "Explore sample size for a chosen confidence interval width.")
```

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

In [Activity: Estimate a population mean with a precision target](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision), what does a full-width target of 4 units mean? Will every simulated interval meet it?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-precision-versus-power">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A full width of 4 units corresponds to a margin of approximately 2 units on either side of the estimated mean. With SD 5, the calculation requires `r precision_n` analyzable patients in total. It meets an anticipated-width target. Individual intervals can be wider or narrower because the sample SD varies across studies.

</details>
:::

## Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval {#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically .advanced-heading}

To interpret one trial, you can compare its confidence interval with both zero and the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold introduced for the chronic pain trial. Zero represents no population difference; the clinical threshold represents the between-group benefit judged worthwhile in this example.

The chronic pain trial illustrates a further use of estimation: interpreting a between-group difference after a trial planned for power. The following three intervals show how the conclusion depends on the values compatible with the data.

```{r clinical-intervals, echo=FALSE}
clinical_intervals <- data.frame(
  lower_pp = c(2, -8, 22),
  upper_pp = c(28, 32, 42),
  interpretation = c(
    "Evidence of benefit; its clinical importance remains uncertain. The interval excludes zero and includes benefits below and above the 20-point threshold.",
    "An inconclusive comparison. Some harm, no difference, small benefits and clinically important benefits remain compatible with the data.",
    "The interval supports a benefit above the clinical threshold. All values in the interval exceed 20 percentage points, under the analysis assumptions."),
  plot_label = c("Benefit; clinical\nimportance uncertain",
    "Inconclusive\ncomparison", "Benefit above\nclinical threshold"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Interval for the difference in relief` = paste(clinical_intervals$lower_pp,
    "to", clinical_intervals$upper_pp, "percentage points"),
  `Clinical conclusion and explanation` = clinical_intervals$interpretation,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Hypothetical 95% intervals for novel minus standard treatment, compared with zero and a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot) places the intervals in Table \@ref(tab:clinical-intervals) on the same scale. Positive differences favor the novel treatment. You can see whether each interval crosses zero, crosses the clinical threshold, or lies entirely below it.

```{r clinical-interval-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Three hypothetical 95% confidence intervals on a common scale. The solid vertical line marks no between-group difference; the dashed line marks the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold. Each horizontal bar spans the stated interval limits.", fig.alt="Three horizontal confidence intervals for novel minus standard treatment. The interval from 2 to 28 percentage points excludes zero but crosses the clinical threshold of 20. The interval from minus 8 to 32 crosses both zero and 20. The interval from 22 to 42 lies entirely above 20."}
par(mar = c(5, 9.1, 4.3, 1), las = 1, bg = "white",
  fg = "#26343d", col.axis = "#26343d", col.lab = "#26343d")
plot(NA, xlim = c(-12, 48), ylim = c(.55, 3.55),
  xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
interval_rows <- 3:1
abline(h = interval_rows, col = "#e5e9ec", lwd = 1)
abline(v = 0, col = "#4b5560", lwd = 1.5)
abline(v = 20, col = "#72428b", lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
axis(1, at = seq(-10, 40, 10), cex.axis = .95)
mtext("Difference in pain-relief percentages", side = 1, line = 2.4)
mtext("Novel minus standard treatment (percentage points)", side = 1,
  line = 3.6, cex = .85)
text(c(0, 20), 3.67, c("No difference\n0", "Clinical threshold\n20"),
  adj = c(.5, 0), cex = .85, xpd = NA)
text(-14, interval_rows, clinical_intervals$plot_label,
  adj = 1, cex = .9, xpd = NA)
segments(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, interval_rows,
  clinical_intervals$upper_pp, interval_rows,
  col = "#17658a", lwd = 3, lend = "butt")
for (limits in list(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, clinical_intervals$upper_pp)) {
  segments(limits, interval_rows - .09, limits, interval_rows + .09,
    col = "#17658a", lwd = 2)
  text(limits, interval_rows + .19, labels = limits, cex = .85)
}
```

For a 95% confidence interval and its corresponding two-sided test, an interval that excludes zero indicates statistical significance at the 5% level. Clinical interpretation also depends on whether the interval lies below, crosses, or lies entirely above the clinical threshold.

These intervals concern the population-level difference between groups; see [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) for the implications for individual patients.

Clinical interpretation also considers harms, burden, and the credibility of the study [@sandoval2025].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-precision">
<summary>Common misconception: high power guarantees clinically useful precision</summary>

A study can detect a difference from zero while leaving considerable uncertainty about whether the benefit is clinically worthwhile. Power concerns the testing decision; precision concerns the interval's width. You can consider both when deciding whether the study can answer the clinical question.

</details>

## Reuse an existing dataset for a different question {#dataset-reuse .advanced-heading}

An existing dataset is another fixed-resource setting, common in bachelor projects. Suppose a completed chronic pain trial included 200 patients and also recorded sleep difficulty before treatment. Your new question is: what percentage of these trial participants reported sleep difficulty at baseline? This differs from the trial's original question about treatment effectiveness.

Baseline sleep information is available for 180 participants; 72 reported difficulty. The observed percentage is 72/180 = 40%. With the sample already fixed, the planning task is to assess the precision the available data can provide.

```{r reused-dataset}
# Estimate a percentage and interval from 72 events among 180 observations.
sleep_result <- single_proportion_interval(events = 72, n = 180,
  confidence = .95)
sleep_result
```

```{r reused-dataset-summary, echo=FALSE}
sleep_limits <- wilson_interval(.40, 180)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Patients in the dataset", "With baseline sleep information",
    "Reporting sleep difficulty", "Observed percentage", "95% Wilson confidence interval"),
  Result = c("200", "180", "72", "40.0%",
    paste(percent(sleep_limits[1, 1]), "to", percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])))),
  caption = "A new descriptive question answered using an existing chronic pain trial dataset.")
```

The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the model. Possible differences between the 20 patients with missing information and those who answered require separate assessment. The trial's eligibility criteria also restrict whom these results describe: its participants may not represent all patients with chronic pain. Random allocation supports the original treatment comparison.

Before analyzing the reused data, you should check that the required variables and time points are available, reuse is permitted, and the analysis fits the new objective. Your report should state the precision needed for the decision and identify analyses developed after inspecting the data as exploratory [@lakens2022; @consortee2025].


::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

For your adapted research question, your plan should identify the new outcome, target population, available sample and missing observations. Would an interval of this width answer your project question? Your report should record these decisions in the [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report), using a fixed-resource estimation goal.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-existing-data">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The new outcome is baseline sleep difficulty. The results directly describe the population defined by the original trial's eligibility criteria. The dataset contains 200 patients, with sleep information for 180 and missing information for 20. Among those with information, 72/180 = 40% reported difficulty; the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 1])` to `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])`.

Whether this precision is useful depends on a decision specified for the project. It may support a broad descriptive estimate, but would not support a requirement to estimate the percentage within 2 percentage points. The report should explain the fixed sample, missing information and restricted population. Adequacy here depends on precision for the descriptive objective.

</details>

:::

## Planning a pilot or feasibility study {#pilot-feasibility .advanced-heading}

So far, feasibility has meant whether you can carry out an informative main study. A preliminary pilot or feasibility study has its own research objectives: investigating whether recruitment, retention, delivery, or other procedures will work. Its sample size should support those decisions.

Suppose a team wants to test a new rehabilitation pathway and needs evidence about recruitment and follow-up. It can recruit 40 patients over three months to investigate these procedures.

Here the sample size should support decisions about recruitment, retention and delivery. The [evidence discussion](#planning-uncertainty) explains how pilot findings can later contribute to planning the definitive trial [@albers2018].

For the pilot, your plan should connect the available resources with the precision needed for these feasibility decisions. The [single-proportion example](#prevalence) explains the corresponding interval-width calculation. Here the hypothetical cap is 40 participants, and expected completion of follow-up is 80%. With 32 of 40 completing follow-up, the observed retention and its interval are shown below.

```{r pilot-retention}
# Estimate retention and its interval from 32 completions among 40 participants.
pilot_retention <- single_proportion_interval(events = 32, n = 40,
  confidence = .95)
pilot_retention
```

```{r pilot-retention-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Completed follow-up`="32/40 (80%)", `95% Wilson confidence interval`=paste(percent(pilot_retention$lower), "to", percent(pilot_retention$upper)), check.names=FALSE), caption="Retention and its uncertainty in a 40-participant feasibility study.")
```

The observed 80% retention still has a wide interval. You can compare it with a prospectively agreed progression criterion and consider reasons for missing outcomes. A point estimate of 80% alone cannot establish that the main trial will retain at least 80%.

Your pilot size should reflect the decision it must support. Ying and colleagues distinguish estimating feasibility with useful precision, assessing progression criteria, detecting practical problems and informing variability for the main trial [@ying2025]. You should specify each outcome's denominator: retention concerns participants enrolled, while a recruitment percentage may concern eligible people approached.

The app below starts with 40 participants and an 80% retention probability. Comparing samples of 40 and 100 shows how more observations affect the uncertainty in the retention estimate. Both retained and non-retained participants contribute when their status is known.

```{r pilot-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pilot_feasibility", "Explore the information a pilot with a fixed number of participants can provide.")
```

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

A pilot's prespecified progression rule requires at least 80% observed retention, a lower 95% confidence limit above 70%, and acceptable delivery. Which of these results meets the numerical criteria: 32 of 40 retained participants, or 80 of 100? Why?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-pilot-progression">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Both samples have 80% observed retention. With 32/40 retained participants, the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 2])`. Its lower limit is below 70%, so it does not meet the numerical progression rule.

With 80/100 retained participants, the interval is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 100)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 100)[1, 2])`. Its lower limit exceeds 70%, so it meets the numerical criteria. Progression would also require acceptable delivery. The larger sample gives a narrower interval around the same retention estimate.

</details>

:::

For another objective, suppose a practical problem independently affects 10% of participants. The probability of observing at least one problem in $n$ participants is $1-(1-0.10)^n$; 29 give at least a 95% probability. Much rarer problems require larger samples for reliable detection. A problem can remain undetected in a small pilot [@ying2025]. Different pilot objectives can therefore imply different numbers.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-goal">
<summary>Common misconception: every pilot needs a treatment-effect power calculation</summary>

A pilot may primarily investigate recruitment, retention or whether procedures are workable. The sample size should support the feasibility questions and provide useful precision for the intended decisions. Planning the definitive trial should combine the pilot findings with relevant external evidence [@albers2018].

</details>

Before writing the protocol, you should check relevant guidance and the current funder's requirements. For examples, [NIHR HTA guidance on feasibility and pilot studies](https://njl-admin.nihr.ac.uk/document/download/2023130) distinguishes feasibility questions from definitive efficacy questions; this is an archived guidance example. The [CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials](https://www.bmj.com/content/355/bmj.i5239) asks for a rationale for pilot numbers and criteria for progression [@nihrfeasibility; @eldridge2016]. Reporting guidance helps you document the design. The sample size method should match the study question and planned analysis.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- An estimate describes a population quantity using sample data; its confidence interval expresses uncertainty.
- A precision target specifies confidence level and interval width.
- Estimation can concern a single population or a between-group difference.
- The justification should explain why the interval width supports the intended decision.

</div>

## Check your understanding {#check-estimation .unnumbered}

```{r quiz-estimation, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_chapter_quiz("estimation-planning")
```

# Exploring power and uncertain assumptions {#curves .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Interpret power curves and distinguish power at an available sample size from the sample required for a power target.
- Justify plausible assumptions using relevant evidence and its uncertainty.
- Assess how event probabilities, outcome variability and available sample size affect power.
- Evaluate feasible design changes when the available sample provides insufficient power.

:::

The calculation in Chapter 2 used a target difference of 30 percentage points. Here, you will examine how power changes if the true difference is smaller or recruitment limits the available sample. Suppose the chronic pain trial can provide 100 analyzable patients per group. The question is what that sample could detect, and which assumptions most affect the answer.

## Reading power curves {#activity-2-can-the-feasible-study-answer-the-question .advanced-heading}

Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves) compares power across sample sizes for three possible population differences. Standard-treatment relief stays at 30%; novel-treatment relief is 45%, 50% or 60%, giving differences of 15, 20 or 30 percentage points. Each curve describes repeated trials under one set of population assumptions [@superpowerbook2022].

The vertical line marks the available 100 analyzable patients per group. The horizontal line marks 90% target power. Recruitment should allow for expected losses separately, using the [recruitment calculation](#account-for-expected-losses).

```{r curve-settings}
# Specify the population assumptions and the available analysis count.
analyzable_cap <- 100
curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = analyzable_cap,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
  width_target = .20)
# Compare three true between-group differences, expressed as probabilities.
effect_sizes <- c(.15, .20, .30)
target_power <- .90
```

```{r power-curves, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Power for true treatment differences of 15, 20 and 30 percentage points, with standard-treatment relief of 30% and two-sided Type I error probability of 5%. Reference lines mark 90% target power and 100 analyzable patients per group.", fig.alt="Power rises with patients per group. At the vertical line of 100, power is about 59%, 83% and 99% for the three differences. The curves reach the horizontal 90% target at 217, 124 and 56 patients per group, respectively."}
# Include all three crossings of the power target in the horizontal range.
curve_table <- power_curve_data(curve_spec, effect_sizes, seq(5, 250, 1))
plot_power_curves(curve_table, target_power, analyzable_cap)
```

<span id="hold-sample-size-fixed-and-vary-the-effect"></span>
<span id="fig:effect-curve"></span>

```{r cap-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cap_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(effect_sizes, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  data.frame(difference = 100 * effect,
    power = percent(spec_power(x, analyzable_cap)),
    required = plan_n(x, target_power = target_power))
}))
knitr::kable(cap_results,
  format = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "html" else "latex",
  col.names = c("True difference (percentage points)",
    "Power with 100 per group", "Patients per group for 90% power"),
  caption = "Power with 100 analyzable patients per group and sample size required for 90% power.")
```

The middle column of Table \@ref(tab:cap-table) corresponds to the intersections with the vertical line at 100 patients per group in Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves). The last column corresponds to the intersections with the horizontal line at 90% power.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-detection-boundary">
<summary>Common misconception: smaller differences cannot be detected</summary>

Power changes gradually with the true difference. A difference below the point where a curve reaches 90% power can still produce a statistically significant result; this happens less often across repeated studies. With 100 patients per group, power is approximately 83% for a 20-point difference and 59% for a 15-point difference.

</details>

The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) connects these curves to the available sample and lets you change the assumptions.

```{r power-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("pain_curves", "Compare power for plausible treatment differences with 100 analyzable patients per group.")
```

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

With 100 analyzable patients per group, which of the three differences would the trial detect with at least 90% power?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curves-predict">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The trial exceeds 90% power for a 30-point difference. Power is approximately 83% for 20 points and 59% for 15 points. Reaching 90% power for these smaller differences would require 124 and 217 patients per group, respectively.

</details>
:::

<span id="model-answer-curve-assumptions"></span>
<span id="model-answer-curves-justify"></span>

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="testing-mechanics">
<summary>How hypothesis tests produce power</summary>

The following examples connect an individual test result to the repeated-study probabilities represented by power curves.

### Does the pilot already answer the clinical question? {#critical-observed-difference .advanced-heading}

For this two-sided comparison, the p-value answers: if the treatments truly had equal population relief probabilities, how likely would the chosen test be to produce a result at least as far from equality as the one observed, in either direction? This calculation also assumes that the statistical model is appropriate. A small p-value provides evidence against equal population relief probabilities under the statistical model.

The pilot's observed 40-percentage-point difference exceeds the 20-percentage-point [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold). But the estimate is uncertain. Using a two-sided comparison of proportions gives a p-value of approximately 0.074. With a Type I error probability of 5%, this does not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis using the chosen test.

What would happen with one more response? If relief with standard treatment remained at 3 of 10 patients, while relief with novel treatment increased from 7 to 8 of 10, the observed difference would increase from 40 to 50 percentage points:

```{r pain-critical-p-values, warning=FALSE}
# Compare the pilot result with one additional treatment response
pain_p_value <- function(novel, standard, n) {
  # x gives relief counts; n gives group sizes. correct = FALSE omits continuity correction.
  prop.test(
    x = c(novel, standard),
    n = c(n, n),
    alternative = "two.sided",
    correct = FALSE
  )$p.value
}

# Compare the two observed results; round p-values to three decimal places.
round(c(
  "7 versus 3" = pain_p_value(7, 3, 10),
  "8 versus 3" = pain_p_value(8, 3, 10)
), 3)
```

```{r pain-critical-p-values-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Novel treatment` = c("7/10 (70%)", "8/10 (80%)"), `Standard treatment` = "3/10 (30%)", `Observed difference` = c("40 percentage points", "50 percentage points"), `p-value` = formatC(c(pain_p_value(7,3,10), pain_p_value(8,3,10)), format="f", digits=3), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Pilot comparisons with seven or eight responses to the novel treatment.")
```

With 8 rather than 7 patients reporting relief, the result becomes statistically significant. For this particular comparison, the smallest observed difference giving $p<0.05$ is therefore $0.8-0.3=0.5$, or 50 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

Notice that the [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) remains 20 percentage points. What patients would consider a worthwhile improvement does not change because your pilot happens to contain only 10 patients per group.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-significance">
<summary>Common misconception: statistical significance decides whether a treatment matters</summary>

A non-significant result can remain compatible with both no effect and a worthwhile benefit. A statistically significant difference can still be too small to matter to patients. You can examine the estimated difference and its [confidence interval](#confidence-interval) against both zero and the clinical threshold.

</details>

*The calculation above uses an approximate test without continuity correction, matching the [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). With such small groups, an exact test may give a different result.*

#### What happens if you recruit more patients? {.advanced-heading}

You can repeat this calculation for larger studies. At each sample size, the observed percentage reporting relief with standard treatment stays at 30%. The calculation identifies the smallest number reporting relief with the novel treatment that gives $p<0.05$.

```{r pain-critical-effect, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Smallest observed improvement giving p < 0.05 at each sample size, conditional on an observed control response of 30%. The two-sided score test uses no continuity correction. Points represent attainable patient counts; connecting lines guide the eye. The hypothetical clinical threshold is 20 percentage points. Counts are analyzable patients before adjustment for dropout.", fig.alt="The smallest observed difference giving statistical significance falls from 50 percentage points at 10 patients per group to 14 at 100 per group. A horizontal line marks the clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The pilot difference of 40 points at 10 patients per group lies below the significance threshold."}
pain_n <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
pain_critical <- vapply(pain_n, function(n) {
  control <- as.integer(round(0.30 * n))
  treatment <- seq.int(control + 1L, n)
  p <- vapply(treatment, function(x) pain_p_value(x, control, n), numeric(1))
  min((treatment[p < 0.05] - control) / n)
}, numeric(1))

local({
  old_par <- par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  plot(pain_n, 100 * pain_critical, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2,
       col = "#17658A", ylim = c(0, 66), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Analyzable patients per group (equal allocation)",
       ylab = "Observed difference in pain relief (percentage points)")
  axis(1, at = pain_n)
  abline(h = 20, col = "#A5500C", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  points(10, 40, pch = 1, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "#303A43")
  legend("topright",
         c("Smallest observed difference with p < 0.05",
           "Clinical threshold: 20 percentage points",
           "Pilot: 7/10 versus 3/10"),
         col = c("#17658A", "#A5500C", "#303A43"),
         lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(16, NA, 1),
         lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
```

With 20 patients per group, an observed difference of 35 percentage points is sufficient for statistical significance under these conditions. With 50 patients per group, the corresponding difference is 20 percentage points. As the sample size increases, smaller observed differences can therefore become statistically significant.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-critical-effect) shows how the observed significance boundary changes. The dashed line shows the clinically meaningful difference chosen for this example. With a larger sample, a result can be statistically significant even when the observed difference is smaller than this clinical threshold. You therefore need to consider the size of the difference and its confidence interval when interpreting the result.

#### How does this relate to power? {.advanced-heading}

The significance boundary concerns an observed result. [Power](#statistical-power) concerns the performance of the planned study: *If the true treatment difference is 30 percentage points, how likely is your study to produce a statistically significant result?*

Different samples will give different observed differences, even when the true treatment effect remains the same. Some will be larger and others smaller. A power calculation takes this variation into account. The [simulation activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) explore this probability across repeated studies.

The observed significance boundary and the true difference used to evaluate power answer different questions [@lakens2022; @superpowerbook2022]. The [clinical interpretation of the interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) considers whether benefits below the clinical threshold remain compatible with the data.

### Type I and Type II error probabilities as areas {#alpha-beta .advanced-heading}

This separate example uses one group to make the error probabilities easier to draw. Imagine repeatedly sampling 25 patients and calculating their mean systolic blood pressure. The curves show the distribution of sample means across repeated studies. One curve assumes a population mean of 120 mmHg; the other assumes 125 mmHg. These are sampling distributions of the mean.

[Standard deviation](#standard-deviation){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SD) describes how much individual patients differ. [Standard error](#standard-error){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SE) describes how much an estimated mean would vary if you repeated the study with new patients. If individual blood pressures have a known SD of 15 mmHg, the mean from 25 independent patients has an SE of $15/\sqrt{25}=3$ mmHg. With 100 patients, the SE falls to 1.5 mmHg. Increasing the sample size reduces the standard error of the mean while the population SD remains fixed.

For this illustration, the null hypothesis specifies a mean of 120 mmHg. A one-sided test looks for an increase, rejecting the null when the sample mean exceeds a cutoff called the critical value. The [two-arm treatment-comparison activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) use [two-sided tests](#two-sided-test).

Under the 120 mmHg curve, the area above the cutoff is the probability of a false positive: the [Type I error probability](#alpha). Under the 125 mmHg curve, the area below the cutoff is the probability of a false negative: the [Type II error probability](#beta). The area under the alternative curve above the cutoff is the true-positive probability, or power. Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-distribution-figure) separates the two assumed populations so that each shaded area has an unambiguous interpretation.

```{r alpha-beta-areas}
# Population means under the null and the specified alternative.
mu0 <- 120
mu1 <- 125
sigma <- 15
n <- 25
alpha <- .05
# sqrt(n) is the square root of n; the mean varies less as n increases.
standard_error <- sigma / sqrt(n)
# For this one-sided example, qnorm() gives the rejection cutoff.
critical <- mu0 + qnorm(1 - alpha) * standard_error
# pnorm() gives the probability below that cutoff under the alternative.
# This is the Type II error probability; its complement is power.
beta <- pnorm(critical, mean = mu1, sd = standard_error)
c(standard_error = standard_error, critical = critical,
  beta = beta, power = 1 - beta)
```

```{r alpha-beta-areas-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Standard error", "Critical mean", "Type I error probability", "Type II error probability", "Power"), Result=c(paste(standard_error,"mmHg"), paste(round(critical,1),"mmHg"), percent(alpha), percent(beta), percent(1-beta))),
  caption = "Error probabilities and power for the specified sampling distributions.")
```

```{r sampling-distribution-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Sampling distributions of the mean with 25 independent observations and known SD 15 mmHg. In the upper panel, the shaded rejection area is Type I error probability. In the lower panel, the shaded non-rejection area is Type II error probability and the shaded rejection area is power.", fig.alt="The upper null curve is centered at 120 and the lower alternative curve at 125 mmHg. Both have standard error 3. The critical mean is about 124.9; Type I error probability is 5 percent and Type II error probability about 49 percent."}
sampling_example <- normal_sampling_operating_characteristics(
  mu0 = mu0, mu1 = mu1, sigma = sigma, n = n, alpha = alpha,
  sidedness = "greater")
plot_sample_mean_distributions(sampling_example)
```

Here the critical mean is about 124.9 mmHg and power is about 51%. Repeating the study at the specified alternative would produce a mean above that threshold about half the time.


```{r errors-app-preview, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_app_preview("alpha_beta", "Move a rejection boundary and explore false positives, false negatives and power.")
```


These areas are calculated directly from a one-sample normal model with a known population SD.


</details>

## Choosing plausible assumptions {#st01-expectations .advanced-heading}

Your assumptions should explain why previous findings apply to the planned study. Four questions help connect that evidence to the calculation [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2]:

- What would happen with the comparator? Disease severity, background care and follow-up can change the control event percentage or outcome variability. Where data are sparse, expert judgment should be identified and its uncertainty examined.
- What could explain an apparent treatment advantage? In observational comparisons, differences in patients, care or diagnosis can contribute to the observed difference. Earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without postponing death; more detailed staging can change which patients are compared within a disease stage.
- What additional benefit would justify the intervention? Patients and clinicians should consider adverse effects, treatment burden and alternatives when judging a clinically worthwhile difference. More demanding treatment may require a larger benefit to justify its use.
- How sensitive is the decision to uncertainty? Plausible ranges should reflect differences between studies and limitations in the evidence. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) shows their implications for required sample size or performance at a fixed count.

The ST01 gastric-cancer surgery trial illustrates these judgments. Its design team used a consensus estimate of 20% five-year survival with conventional (D1) surgery. Apparent advantages of more extensive (D2) surgery in Japanese observational studies could partly reflect earlier diagnosis, more detailed staging, or differences in patients' age and fitness. D2 also carried additional postoperative risks, so the anticipated survival gain needed to justify these harms [@fayers2000beliefs]. The table distinguishes the calculation target from expectations and clinical judgments elicited from 26 surgeons before recruitment.

| Planning role | Reported value and basis |
|:--|:--|
| Anticipated difference | The wider survey anticipated a 9.4-percentage-point survival advantage; the three design-committee surgeons anticipated 13.1 points. |
| Target difference | The detailed calculation used 13.5 points, from 20% to 33.5% survival, giving 400 patients at 90% power. It reflected the design committee's expectations. |
| Clinical importance | The wider survey's average interval of clinical indecision was 4.6–10.8 points. Its upper boundary represented sufficient benefit to favor D2, given the operation's additional risks. Individual judgments varied. |

Table: (\#tab:st01-planning-roles) ST01 planning roles: absolute between-group differences in five-year survival, expressed in percentage points [@fayers2000beliefs].

The survey left the original design unchanged; its clinical boundaries summarize individual surgeons' judgments. Reproducing ST01 requires its survival-analysis method. More generally, differences in patients or care may change the assumed outcomes, while treatment harms inform what benefit is worthwhile. The sample-size consequences depend on those resulting inputs and the chosen analysis.

<span id="planning-uncertainty"></span>

Investigators can overestimate how readily a trial will meet its operational targets. In a prospective survey, investigators assigned an average probability of 78.8% to meeting their recruitment target. Among the 281 trials with evaluable recruitment outcomes, 42.7% met that target. For completing primary data collection on time, the average predicted probability was 72.2%, whereas 13.4% of 536 evaluated trials finished on time. The denominators differ because outcome information was available for different sets of trials. These findings support examining a slower recruitment scenario when using the [screening and enrollment funnel](#recruitment-feasibility) [@benjamin2022forecasts].

<details class="reading-note">
<summary>About the forecast survey</summary>

The survey received responses from 740 principal investigators, a response percentage of 16.7%. Outcome follow-up was incomplete. These features limit how widely its findings can be generalized [@benjamin2022forecasts].

</details>

Uncertainty remains even when assumptions are carefully justified. In a review of 107 randomized trials, the median [standardized treatment effect](#standardized-treatment-effect) used as the calculation target was 0.30, compared with a median observed effect of 0.11 [@rothwell2018targets]. Differences between targets and results can reflect uncertain treatment effects and sampling variability. Assessing investigator optimism also requires evidence about beliefs and their uncertainty before results are known [@liu2024uncertainty].

For your study, earlier observations and elicited expectations can inform a plausible range of population differences. Their values, the target difference and the clinical threshold can coincide or follow a different order. The chosen target needs evidence of plausibility and clinical importance. When a target exceeds the benefit supported by the evidence, your justification should examine power at smaller plausible differences. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) makes these implications visible [@cook2018delta2].

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="further-planning-approaches">
<summary>Planning with uncertainty about the true difference</summary>

The sensitivity analyses above examine separate fixed scenarios. Other methods incorporate uncertainty about the true difference directly into the planning criterion:

- Safeguard power uses uncertainty in a previous difference estimate when planning. It can imply a much larger sample when the evidence is weak [@perugini2014].
- Bayesian and hybrid approaches can average performance over a justified distribution of plausible parameter values. Assurance or expected power answers a different question from power at one fixed difference; the distribution and decision rule need justification [@kunzmann2021review; @pezeshk2003].

These approaches require a justified uncertainty distribution or adjustment and a method suited to the planned analysis.

A review of Bayesian randomized trials found that hybrid sample-size methods were common and fully Bayesian methods were rarely used [@marks2026]. A Bayesian trial can use a fixed sample size or prespecified adaptations. Its planning method should reflect the chosen decision rule; the [adaptive-design discussion](#sample-size-re-estimation) explains the additional decisions to document.

</details>

## Sensitivity to other assumptions {#stress-test-the-study-plan .advanced-heading}

<span id="compare-planning-assumptions"></span>
<span id="tab:pain-core-sensitivity"></span>

A [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis){.no-glossary-tooltip} examines what happens when a planning assumption changes within a plausible range. The earlier curves varied the true treatment difference. Figure \@ref(fig:assumption-sensitivity) now keeps that difference fixed and examines two other inputs.

For the chronic pain trial, standard-treatment relief might differ from 30%. The left panel examines the 20-point difference from the earlier curves, keeping it fixed while changing the two relief probabilities together. For a continuous outcome, the variability of individual scores might be greater than anticipated. The right panel keeps the mean difference at 3 units and varies the common standard deviation. Both panels use 100 analyzable patients per group, so changes in power reflect the changed population assumptions.

```{r assumption-sensitivity, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Sensitivity at 100 analyzable patients per group and a two-sided Type I error probability of 5%. Left: the between-group relief difference stays at 20 percentage points while standard-treatment relief varies. Right: the mean difference stays at 3 units while the common standard deviation varies. Dots mark standard-treatment relief of 30% and SD 5; dashed lines mark 90% target power.", fig.alt="Two panels use power from 0 to 100 percent vertically. The left varies standard-treatment relief from 10 to 60 percent, adding 20 points for novel treatment; power changes with the event probabilities. The right varies the common SD from 4 to 9 at a mean difference of 3; power falls as variability increases."}
# Hold both sample sizes and treatment differences fixed.
binary_curve_spec <- curve_spec
binary_curve_spec$p_treatment <- .50
mean_curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "means", n = analyzable_cap,
  delta = 3, sd = 5)
draw_assumption_sensitivity(binary_curve_spec, mean_curve_spec, target_power)
```

<span id="fig:pain-target-sensitivity-plot"></span>

```{r pain-target-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
baseline_scenarios <- lapply(c(.10, .30, .50), function(p) {
  x <- binary_curve_spec; x$p_control <- p; x$p_treatment <- p + .20; x
})
sd_scenarios <- lapply(c(5, 7, 9), function(sd) {
  x <- mean_curve_spec; x$sd <- sd; x
})
alternatives <- c(baseline_scenarios, sd_scenarios)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Assumption = c("Relief: standard 10%, novel 30%", "Relief: standard 30%, novel 50%",
    "Relief: standard 50%, novel 70%", "Mean difference 3; SD 5",
    "Mean difference 3; SD 7", "Mean difference 3; SD 9"),
  `Power with 100 per group` = percent(vapply(alternatives, spec_power, numeric(1))),
  `Patients per group for 90% power` = vapply(alternatives,
    function(x) plan_n(x, target_power = target_power), numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Sensitivity to event probabilities and outcome variability. The mean comparison uses a pooled two-sample t-test calculation.")
```

<span id="tab:fixed-plan-sensitivity"></span>

For binary outcomes, the event probabilities determine variability, so the same absolute difference can give different power. For continuous outcomes, a larger standard deviation makes the specified mean difference harder to detect. Relevant evidence should support the alternatives and their ranges [@cook2018delta2; @candel2023].

The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) provides the corresponding controls. Its Description explains how the calculated curves and simulated studies relate. Your supporting study plan should record the alternatives that affect the decision. For example, the BEP protocol presents its principal calculation in the main text and alternative assumptions in an additional file [@wang2024bep]. DELTA² and CONSORT recommend documenting sensitivity to calculation inputs [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025].

## When the available sample is insufficient {#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose .advanced-heading}

### Underpowered studies {#underpowered-studies .advanced-heading}

An underpowered study has a low probability of obtaining a statistically significant result when the specified difference is present in the population. For the chronic pain trial with 100 patients per group, power is about 59% if the true difference is 15 percentage points. Across repeated trials under these assumptions, approximately 41% would fail to detect that difference.

In underpowered studies, sampling variability can be large relative to the treatment difference. Studies that obtain statistically significant results favoring treatment tend to have unusually large estimates of its benefit. Focusing on those significant results can therefore exaggerate the apparent benefit [@gelman2014beyond].

Larger samples reduce [sampling variability](#sampling-variability). Addressing bias requires attention to the design, measurement and analysis.

### Ways to increase power {#increase-power .advanced-heading}

Before collecting data, you can consider whether the design could provide more information about the treatment effect. Table \@ref(tab:increase-power) summarizes changes to recruitment, measurement and analysis.

Power can improve through more informative measurements, appropriate use of baseline information, and a design that makes efficient treatment comparisons. Which changes help depends on the outcome, allocation and planned analysis. Covariate adjustment can improve efficiency for binary, ordinal and time-to-event outcomes as well as continuous outcomes [@fda2023covariates]. The continuous-outcome calculations in @candel2023 illustrate the roles of allocation, baseline information and within-person comparisons.

| Option | Why it can help | What to consider |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Increase the analyzable sample | More independent patients reduce sampling variability at the same true difference. | Another center or a longer recruitment period could supply more patients. [Multicenter planning](#multicenter-trials) should reflect allocation within centers and the intended analysis. |
| Improve follow-up and outcome completeness | More recorded outcomes preserve the analyzable sample. | Accessible follow-up and reminders can help. Reasons for missing outcomes inform the missing-data analysis. |
| Improve measurement | Reliable measurements reduce noise and support more informative comparisons. | A consistent definition and assessment time matter for pain relief. A different outcome needs its own calculation. |
| Use an efficient design and analysis | Informative baseline measurements or appropriate paired comparisons can improve precision and power. | Adjustment should be prespecified. A [crossover trial](#crossover-trial) requires suitable treatment reversibility, disease stability and control of carryover. |
| Keep allocation balanced when appropriate | With equal variances, equal group sizes efficiently use a fixed total for a two-means comparison. | Other outcome distributions or design requirements can justify a different allocation and matching calculation. |

Table: (\#tab:increase-power) Design changes that can improve power and their planning implications.

Changing the Type I error probability or using a one-sided test changes the rejection rule. A higher Type I error probability increases both power and false-positive probability. A one-sided test concentrates rejection in a prespecified direction. These choices need scientific justification before data collection [@moye2002].

<span id="model-answer-larger-study-resources"></span>

### Decisions with a fixed sample {#available-sample .advanced-heading}

The chronic pain example provides 100 analyzable patients per group. It exceeds the 90% power target at a 30-point difference, but power at the clinically important 20-point difference is about 83%. If 90% power at 20 points is essential, the calculation requires 124 analyzable patients per group. The [Sample size reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) lets you examine how changing the available count affects that conclusion.

Your justification should state the available sample, the plausible assumptions and the power they imply. The next decision is whether additional recruitment or a scientifically appropriate design change is feasible. A revised research objective should be agreed before data collection and supported by its own calculation.

<span id="a-fixed-total-of-70-patients"></span>
<span id="sensitivity-is-not-observed-post-hoc-power"></span>

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-observed-power">
<summary>Common misconception: power calculated from the observed effect explains the completed study</summary>

Substituting the study's observed effect into a power calculation adds no independent evidence about that same result. Interpretation of a completed study uses the estimate, confidence interval, design and limitations, as explained in [clinical interpretation](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically). Sensitivity analysis assesses the design using independently justified population assumptions [@consortee2025; @lakens2022].

</details>

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Power at an available sample and sample size required for a power target are two readings of the same curves.
- Relevant evidence and its uncertainty should support the plausible assumptions examined.
- Event probabilities and outcome variability affect power even when the treatment difference stays fixed.
- When power is insufficient, the planning decision concerns feasible recruitment, design changes or a justified revision of the objective.

</div>
